questions.question: Maradona's Hand of God goal stood in 1986 because the referee could not see it. What has changed since?
options: Handball was legalised for attacking players in 1992
VAR now reviews every goal for handball automatically
Referees were given the power to consult the crowd
A second referee was added behind each goal line
questions.answer: VAR now reviews every goal for handball automatically
questions.explanation: Every goal is now checked by video officials, and a handball in the build-up disallows it regardless of intent. Maradona's goal would not survive thirty seconds of review. He admitted it years later, saying it was scored a little with the head and a little with the hand of God. VAR arrived at the World Cup in 2018 and remains divisive, with many arguing it has broken the rhythm of celebration.
questions.memory_hook: Every goal now gets video-checked for handball in the build-up, so the Hand of God would last about thirty seconds today. Maradona admitted it eventually, saying it came a little from his head and a little from the hand of God. VAR came to the World Cup in 2018.

questions.question: The Bay of Pigs invasion failed within three days in 1961. What did Kennedy withhold at the last moment?
options: Promised American air cover for the landing force
Intelligence on the location of Cuban forces
Funding, which was cut the week before departure
Weapons, leaving the brigade with training rifles
questions.answer: Promised American air cover for the landing force
questions.explanation: The CIA plan depended on airstrikes destroying Castro's air force. Kennedy, wanting deniability, cut the second wave, so surviving Cuban aircraft sank the supply ships and strafed the beaches. Around 1,200 exiles surrendered and were later ransomed for $53 million in food and medicine. The humiliation pushed Castro toward Moscow and directly set up the missile crisis eighteen months later.
questions.memory_hook: The plan needed airstrikes to wipe out Castro's air force. Kennedy cancelled the second wave for deniability, so surviving Cuban planes sank the supply ships. 1,200 exiles surrendered and were ransomed for $53 million in food and medicine. It pushed Castro to Moscow and led straight to the missile crisis.

questions.question: The Parthenon stood largely intact for over two thousand years. What destroyed most of it?
options: A Venetian shell hit Ottoman gunpowder stored inside
An earthquake brought down the roof in the 1600s
Lord Elgin's removal crew collapsed the eastern wall
Ottoman forces dismantled it for building material
questions.answer: A Venetian shell hit Ottoman gunpowder stored inside
questions.explanation: In 1687 the Ottomans were using the Parthenon as a powder magazine during a Venetian siege, on the reasonable assumption nobody would shell a temple. A mortar round found it and the explosion blew out the centre of the building. It had survived as a temple, then a church, then a mosque, essentially intact until that moment. Elgin removed the sculptures over a century later, which Greece still disputes.
questions.memory_hook: The Ottomans stored gunpowder in it during a Venetian siege in 1687, assuming nobody would shell a temple. A mortar found it and blew the middle out. It had been intact as temple, then church, then mosque for 2,100 years until that one shot. Elgin took the marbles a century later.

questions.question: Mao's Great Leap Forward aimed to industrialise China rapidly. What made the famine so severe?
options: Farmers deliberately destroyed crops as a form of protest
Foreign powers blockaded all grain imports into China
Officials reported fake harvests, so grain was over-taken
A drought destroyed three consecutive rice harvests
questions.answer: Officials reported fake harvests, so grain was over-taken
questions.explanation: Local cadres competed to report record yields, terrified of being labelled rightist. The state then requisitioned grain based on those inflated figures, taking food that did not exist and leaving villages with nothing. Peasants were also pulled off farms to smelt useless pig iron in backyard furnaces, melting down their own tools. Estimates of the death toll run from 15 to 45 million, largely between 1959 and 1961.
questions.memory_hook: Officials competed to report fake record harvests because being called a rightist was dangerous. The state then took grain based on those invented numbers, leaving villages nothing. Meanwhile farmers were smelting their own tools into useless pig iron in backyard furnaces. Somewhere between 15 and 45 million died.

questions.question: The Olympic torch relay was introduced at the 1936 Berlin Games. Who devised it?
options: Greek officials, as a condition of hosting rights
Nazi organisers, as propaganda linking Germany to Greece
The International Olympic Committee, reviving an ancient rite
Baron de Coubertin, for the first modern Games in 1896
questions.answer: Nazi organisers, as propaganda linking Germany to Greece
questions.explanation: The relay was designed by Carl Diem for the 1936 Games to draw a line from ancient Greece to the Third Reich, and Leni Riefenstahl filmed it for Olympia. Ancient Greek games had a sacred flame but no relay of this kind. The route from Olympia to Berlin also traced ground German forces would later cover. It has been kept ever since, generally without the origin being mentioned.
questions.memory_hook: Carl Diem invented it for Berlin 1936 to link the Third Reich to ancient Greece, and Riefenstahl filmed it. The ancient games had a flame but no relay. The route from Olympia to Berlin crossed ground German armies would later take. Every Games has done it since, origin usually unmentioned.

questions.question: David Lynch's Eraserhead took five years to finish. How did he keep it going?
options: A film school grant covered the entire production
He sold the rights to his next three films in advance
He funded it with a paper round and slept on the set
A studio bankrolled it after seeing twenty minutes
questions.answer: He funded it with a paper round and slept on the set
questions.explanation: Lynch shot at the American Film Institute over five years, funded partly by delivering the Wall Street Journal, with Jack Nance keeping the same haircut throughout so shots would match. Lynch lived on the set. It found an audience through midnight screenings, which is how Mel Brooks saw it and hired him for The Elephant Man. Lynch never explained what the baby was made of and took the answer with him.
questions.memory_hook: Five years at the AFI, funded partly by a Wall Street Journal paper round, with Jack Nance keeping the same haircut the whole time so the shots would cut together. Lynch slept on the set. Midnight screenings got it seen, Mel Brooks watched it and hired him for The Elephant Man.

questions.question: Otis Redding wrote Respect in 1965, but Aretha Franklin's 1967 version is the one people know. What did she change?
options: She flipped it from a man pleading to a woman demanding
She recorded it with Redding singing backing vocals
She rewrote the lyrics entirely, keeping only the title
She slowed it into a gospel ballad with no rhythm section
questions.answer: She flipped it from a man pleading to a woman demanding
questions.explanation: Redding's original is a man asking his wife for respect when he gets home. Franklin, arranging with her sisters, reversed the power entirely and added the spelled-out chorus and the sock it to me line, neither of which existed before. It became an anthem for both civil rights and women's liberation. Redding reportedly said at Monterey that a girl had taken his song away from him, and meant it admiringly.
questions.memory_hook: Redding's version is a man asking his wife for respect at home. Franklin flipped who holds the power, and added both the spelling and sock it to me, neither of which was in the original. Redding said a girl had stolen his song, and meant it as a compliment.

questions.question: Tootsie (1982) has Dustin Hoffman playing an actor disguised as a woman. What did Hoffman say the role taught him?
options: He learned he preferred comedy to dramatic roles
He decided never to work with a director he had not met
He realised how many women he would never have spoken to
He found the makeup process physically unbearable
questions.answer: He realised how many women he would never have spoken to
questions.explanation: Hoffman has described asking the makeup team to make him beautiful, being told this was as good as it got, and going home and weeping. His realisation was that he had spent his life not talking to interesting women because they did not meet a standard he had absorbed without examining. He described the film as a comedy that was never funny to him. It was nominated for ten Oscars and Jessica Lange won Supporting Actress.
questions.memory_hook: Hoffman asked the makeup team to make him beautiful, was told that was as good as it got, went home and cried. His conclusion was that he had spent his life ignoring interesting women who did not meet a standard he had never examined. He said the comedy was never funny to him.

questions.question: The Tigris and Euphrates both rise in Turkey and flow through Iraq. What tension does that create?
options: Both rivers change course across the border annually
Neither country recognises the other's river borders
Turkish dams control how much water reaches downstream
The rivers flow in opposite directions half the year
questions.answer: Turkish dams control how much water reaches downstream
questions.explanation: Turkey's Southeastern Anatolia Project involves more than twenty dams on the headwaters, giving it substantial control over flows into Syria and Iraq. Downstream states have no equivalent leverage and there is no binding treaty. Iraqi flows have dropped sharply, and the southern marshes, once drained by Saddam Hussein and partially restored, are shrinking again. Mesopotamia means the land between the rivers, and it is where cities were invented.
questions.memory_hook: Turkey's Anatolia Project put over twenty dams on the headwaters, so it decides what reaches Syria and Iraq, and there is no binding treaty. Iraqi flows have fallen hard and the southern marshes are drying again. Mesopotamia means between the rivers, and it is where cities began.

questions.question: What is the name of the star closest to our solar system?
options: Sirius
Alpha Centauri A
Proxima Centauri
Barnard's Star
questions.explanation: Proxima Centauri is the closest known star to our solar system, at about 4.24 light-years away. It is a red dwarf star and part of the Alpha Centauri triple star system. Proxima Centauri has a potentially habitable planet, Proxima b, in its orbit. Even at the speed of our fastest spacecraft, it would take over 75,000 years to reach Proxima Centauri.
questions.memory_hook: Proxima Centauri = closest star, 4.24 light-years away. Traveling at NASA's New Horizons spacecraft speed (58,000 km/h), it would take 78,000 years to get there. Our nearest neighbor is impossibly far by any human standard of distance.

questions.question: Uluru rises 348 metres from the Australian desert. How much of it is underground?
options: Roughly half, matching what is visible above the ground
Most of it, extending several kilometres below the surface
About a tenth, anchoring it against the desert winds
Almost none, since it sits on a shallow bed of hard clay
questions.answer: Most of it, extending several kilometres below the surface
questions.explanation: Uluru is the exposed tip of a rock slab that continues an estimated 2.5km underground, tilted almost vertical by ancient tectonic folding, so what is visible is a small fraction of the whole. It is arkose sandstone, and the orange colour is surface iron oxidation; freshly broken rock is grey. Climbing was permanently banned in 2019 at the request of the Anangu traditional owners, for whom the site is sacred.
questions.memory_hook: Uluru is the tip of a slab running an estimated 2.5km down, tilted nearly vertical by ancient folding, so most of it is buried. The orange is just rusted surface iron; break it open and it is grey. Climbing was banned in 2019 at the request of the Anangu traditional owners.

questions.question: Stem cells can become other cell types, but not all are equally flexible. What can an embryonic stem cell do that an adult one cannot?
options: Survive outside the body without a nutrient medium
Become any cell type in the entire body
Repair damaged DNA in neighbouring cells
Divide without any limit on the number of times
questions.answer: Become any cell type in the entire body
questions.explanation: Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent, able to become any of the roughly 200 cell types. Adult stem cells are multipotent, restricted to a family, so bone marrow stem cells make blood cells but not neurons. Shinya Yamanaka showed in 2006 that ordinary adult cells could be reprogrammed back to a pluripotent state by adding four genes, winning the 2012 Nobel and sidestepping much of the ethical objection to embryonic sources.
questions.memory_hook: Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent and can become any of about 200 cell types. Adult ones are restricted to a family, so marrow makes blood but not neurons. Yamanaka showed in 2006 you can reprogram ordinary adult cells back to pluripotent with four genes, which won a Nobel and dodged the ethics fight.
